claims.claim: Insurance works by pooling risk: a risk pool combines many people's medical costs to set premiums, letting the higher costs of the less healthy be offset by the lower costs of the healthy, with larger, more stable pools yielding more predictable premiums.
A premium is the amount paid (typically monthly) to keep coverage regardless of care used; a deductible is what the enrollee pays for covered services before the plan starts to pay.
A copayment is a fixed dollar amount for a covered service paid after the deductible; coinsurance is a percentage (e.g., 20%) of a covered service's allowed amount paid after the deductible.

The out-of-pocket maximum is the most an enrollee pays for covered in-network services in a plan year; after it is reached the plan pays 100% of covered benefits, and it does not include premiums, non-covered services, or out-of-network care.
For a plan with a $2,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum, an enrollee with $50,000 of covered in-network allowed charges pays $6,000 total and the plan pays $44,000.
A network is the facilities, providers, and suppliers a plan has contracted with; in-network care costs less, and out-of-network care costs more or is not covered.

HMOs usually limit coverage to in-network care (except emergencies) and often require referrals; PPOs also cover out-of-network care at higher cost with no referral; EPOs cover in-network only, typically without referrals; POS plans give in-network savings but require referrals to specialists.

ACA Marketplace plans must cover ten categories of essential health benefits (including outpatient, emergency, hospitalization, maternity/newborn, mental health and substance use, prescription drugs, rehabilitative/habilitative, lab, preventive/chronic-disease management, and pediatric services with dental and vision) and cover certain preventive services at no cost.
Prior authorization is approval a plan may require before covering a service or prescription; a formulary is the list of prescription drugs a plan covers.

In 2023, 92.0% of US people had coverage for some or all of the year and 8.0% (about 26.4 million) were uninsured; employment-based coverage was most common at 53.7%, direct-purchase 10.2%, Medicare 18.9%, and Medicaid 18.9%.
Cost-sharing percentages apply to the plan's allowed amount (negotiated rate), not the provider's original charge.

conflictingEvidence.issue: A larger risk pool is sometimes assumed to guarantee lower premiums.
positions: Larger pools make premiums more predictable and stable.
Premium level depends on the average health cost of the pool's enrollees, so a large pool of high-cost members can still have high premiums.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that larger, stable pools make premiums more predictable (not necessarily lower), following the American Academy of Actuaries.

sourceRecords.title: Risk Pooling: How Health Insurance in the Individual Market Works
sourceRecords.notes: Professional actuarial body. Supports the risk-pooling mechanism ('a group of individuals whose medical costs are combined to calculate premiums'; pooling lets higher costs of the less healthy be offset by lower costs of the healthy; larger pools are more predictable and stable) and defines adverse selection and the premium spiral. Read the full page via curl with a browser user-agent. Copyrighted; synthesized in original prose, not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What Health Insurance Risk Pooling Is, and Why It's Key to Maintaining Affordability
sourceRecords.notes: Secondary explainer corroborating that risk pooling spreads cost across healthy and sicker individuals so higher-risk costs are subsidized by lower-risk members, and that broader pooling improves affordability. Content confirmed via WebSearch summary of the Commonwealth Fund explainer. Copyrighted; used only as corroboration and synthesized, not reproduced.
